review_body: I gave this three stars based on my last Stant gas cap.  It's plastic, with an inexpensive cylinder lock.  There isn't anything special about it.  My fist one was a Mopar branded Stant.  The second was an actual Stant, and now I'm on my third.  They're on my 2005 Dodge Ram 2500 with a 5.9L Cummins.  They only last a few years. The worst part is when I have to get it off, it isn't that difficult to use a similarly shaped key with the same grooves in it to force the tumblers to give way... which is why I end up buying a new one.  Until something better comes about, they're better than non-locking caps.  The good thing is that this cost me half of what Advanced Auto Parts wanted, not including my state's sales tax.  EDIT: After four years, the lock cylinder now comes out of the hole it rotates in.  I'm not sure if the tumblers are stuck, but WD-40 nor liquid graphite helps.  So, as long as I keep the lock cylinder on the key, insert and turn, I can remove the fuel cap to get fuel.  I'll be looking for another cap, if I can find one that isn't the same style.

product_title: 2-bike Bicycle Car Truck Hitch Rack
review_body: originally bought mine from prohoists themselves but thought I'd share some thoughts.  first off, IT WORKS.  It hauls 2 bikes (more if you want to squeeze and don't mind that there are only 2 carrying pads/straps.  The arms seem sturdy.  I'm no welder but the welds appears solid.  I don't remember how the instructions were (if there were any) but I remember not being impressed.  regardless, comes with a 1.25 to 2 inch adapter if you need.  The swing arm pin wire brace is very tight.  I put a small spring clip and lanyard on it to make it easier to pull.  The hitch rack folds down as a unit with the pivot point at the bottom of the mast.  The rack arms DO NOT swing down.  The mast has a screw hitch bolt with a nut inside the mast base so the mast is anchored into the hitch nice and tight.  The top arm needed to be installed onto the mast.  There are 2 bolts, 2 washers and 2 locking nuts (I think the pre-applied thread locker stuff).  The mast and top arms don't fit flush and others of this same make/OEM have seen similar issues).  So after install and locking the nuts down tight (the mast bolt holes are oversized),  the gap between mast and arm unit gives a bit of play and wagging.  I have never had a problem with the rack or with driving but it is definiately not a trivial amount of wag.  Once again no problems but it is usually better to distribute the torque of the bikes along the entire interface between the mast and arm unit than just at pivot points inside of the interface.  So far the metal is holding up.  To improved the interface 2 years later, I diassembled it, cleaned and slapped on epoxy putty (~$8, JB weld type stuff) around the mast (taking care to put none above or on top of the bolt holes.  As I pushed the arm unit down onto the mast, a lot of the putty gets pushed down (I hope some stayed between the two parts) and I kept reforming the extra puty around the bottom of the arm unit as it slid (with some force) down.  put the bolts in (quickly) to makesure the holes were good and aligned (remember - working time with epoxy) and formed the remaining putty around the bottom of the arm unit and mast edge.  This makes a big glop of epoxy that surrouds the bottom of the interface (a good thing).  It dried to metal hard as usual.  Hopefully this improves the force loading interface.  Once again, I don't think I needed to do this but it makes me feel better.  important to note the following: the velcro straps wear out after about 2 years a decent amount.  depending on the air flow around your car (I have a low coupe - with a hitch...I know), the bikes and the pads that are on may get pushed to the back edge of the rack.  This always makes me nervous so I always use a bungee cord to keep the bike close to the mast (better load mechanics anyway).  finally the bolts rust superficially as do some of the joints.  I rec spray paint for cosmesis as well as protection at the areas you start to see the rust.

product_title: Motorcycle Alarm with Remote Engine Start - Universal: Will FIT ALL Motorcycles Suzuki, Honda, Yamaha, Kawasaki, Ducati, Harley Davidson
review_headline: Overwhelming at first, but really easy after all :D
review_body: ~My Experience~  I read the other comments and was a little worried about my ability to do this myself, but bought it regardless. I downloaded a service manual from the Internet for my bike so I could study the wiring diagram. Then I studied the pseudo-diagram that the alarm instructions provided. The colors of the BIKE-SIDE wires it said were obviously not the same, if it said connect it with the Brown wire that came from the ignition and went to the CDI, I looked for the color of wire that went from here to there on the Service manual diagram - red/black. So, I was able to install it easily without any troubles. I can say that the remote start wire (blue wire of this product) is according to the instructions go to the \\"start line\\". After studying the service manual, I suggest that it's connected to the output wire of the start switch/button (assuming that switch leads to a relay). This will allow the remote OR the start switch to start the engine.  ~Review~  Overall, excellent, super-affordable kit that works great. It'll trip the alarm from a small nudge to the handlebar grip, but won't trip from the wind blowing. :) Also, the remotes work from around 100 meters away.  ~Recommendations~  I recommend that anyone who buys this to study the kinda-okay diagram provided with it. That diagram makes much more sense while studying the wiring diagram of your bike alongside it. With a bit of patience and confidence, you'll have an alarm up in no time. If you are still psyched out about doing it yourself, taking it to your local motorcycle service shop will work fine, too. :)    - Mykel

product_title: Black Metro 3D Flexible Carbon Fiber Vinyl Wrap Film 24"x12"
review_headline: Not sure why the other reviewer is displeased...
review_body:
I'll be the first to admit, this vinyl cannot hold a candle to 3-M's Di-Noc. But Di-Noc is also quite a bit more expensive than this. For the price you pay, you get a good quality material. I've used this on several surfaces, and if you have a bit of patience, you can get really, really good results. Believe me, I've spent hours applying this to everything from my computer case to USB flash drives. If you have a hair dryer, it makes applying it that much easier. Don't get me wrong. A heat source isn't necessary, but it does make life easier.

Its textured, so you get that shifting color depending upon how light hits it. Really nice. The texture is also reasonably good to the hand.

The area this falls short compared to Di-Noc is with bubbles. Di-Noc has channels on the glue side so that air pockets can escape after you apply it. This is really, really convenient. This on the other hand is a more traditional vinyl in that the bottom is flat. This is where that patience I spoke of comes into play. All you have to to is be sure you don't miss a spot when applying pressure, and you will end up with good results. On smaller pieces I've done, I ended up with no bubbles, while on my computer case, I ended up with a handful (I got impatient...).

If you don't mind taking your time with a product, this will work fine for most people. If you are in the market for a vinyl that an idiot could apply blindfolded, save your self a bit of time and pick up some Di-Noc. You won't regret it.

UPDATE (8/07/12) It has been a little over 6 months, and I have not experienced any peeling or other degradation on any of my items. I will admit most of them don't get handled frequently, but the glue has stuck firmly to all items. If given the need, I'd buy this film again. I will update again if something starts degrading.

product_title: T10 194 Wedge Base 1.5W LED Bulb with 15xSMD3528 12VDC (6-Pack), Warm White, 1415WWx6
review_headline: May not work well on landscape lighting
review_body:
I had purchased similar wedge based LED items from another place, supXXbright. So this review is a head to head comparison of the two in the landscape lighting.

Appearance-wise, they look pretty much identical. They both have 15 tiny LED bulbs, 3 on the top, and 3 on each side (four sides total). T10, which is sold in Amazon here, has white plastic wedge base while supXXbright has black plastic wedge base.

But once I plug the bulbs into my light fixtures, I can tell they are different. T10 is much dimmer than supXXbright. T10 still give you warm light but it is not as warm as supXXbright. I do have to look carefully to tell the difference though.

BTW, if I look directly into the T10, I can tell its LED bulbs are flickering which is not happening in supXXbright. I have a 100W transformer and my total watts are bellow 35. So this flickering is not due to voltage drop. Again, I do have to look carefully to tell.

The description of T10 says it is for the boat and supXXbright, landscape. So trying T10 on the landscape lighting may not be a right choice.

supXXbright is about 2 bucks cheaper but they do charge S&H. And they are not in Amazon.

I think I will pass T10 till I get a boat :)

review_headline: Beware the Raider with this Computer!
review_body: I was already running Cobra's closed-loop RI 2000 computer on my Yamaha Raider, but I decided to upgrade to this computer so I would never have to wonder if my settings were right.  After fifty miles of easy riding to let the computer discover my K&N air filter and modified air box, not to mention my Cobra 2-into-1 pipe, my mighty 1900cc engine was ready for performance testing.  Did it make a difference?  YES!!!  I putted off the starting line and then gave it a moderate turn of the throttle.  It responded smoothly and firmly, and being the conservative person I am, I floored it.  The Raider responded with jaw-dropping acceleration that forced me to issue maniacal laughter as I rapidly entered hyper-space passing every vehicle in sight having inadvertently issued a trans-warp injection burn.  I looked at the speedo and I was doing over 120mph in 4th gear after only a few seconds, and so I decided that I might want to back her down some.  Subsequent testing proved that even compared to the older Cobra computer, she was much more docile at low speeds and could make hyperspace in less than five seconds from a dead stop.  This computer really does live up to what it says it is.  And the Raider.....well....that's a matter of personal preference.  But none of my Harley's could even touch the kind of performance I'm getting with this bike.  I still love my Harley's though, but not because they can catch me on my Raider.  Bwaaaaaaa.

product_title: Neiko Tools USA Precision Oiler
review_headline: All I can say is they must-have-been SMOK'N!
review_body: I read all the reviews, even the ones that weren't Neiko, because it seemed to good to be true.   I'm sure even the negative review were true for the people that wrote them,  but with a 4 out of 5 stars overall rating, I figured the odds were in my favor, and they were!  When I assembled the upper to the lower halves, I saw a potential for leakage. The internal thread needed to be 0.040 deeper to hide the o-ring between the two halves in order to insure no leak.   I tested the oiler with four gun oils and olive oil.  The performance was excellent with all of them.   A couple review didn't recommend oil with Teflon (PTFE)formulation. Three of the oils I used included Teflon(PTFE). REM oil, Slick ONE, and Breakfree CLP, and they all worked fine.  My personal choice for most applications is REM oil which has the consistency of sewing machine oil. Other reviews stated the oiler worked better with heavier oils but they did not mention what they considered heavy oil.  I found all the oils I tested to work equally as well. I could lay down a dot, smaller than the head on a common pin with pin-point accruacy, to as much oil as I wanted, depending on how many times I pushed down on the plunger.  When the plunger was not pressed, the oil flow would shut-off completely (as tested, no leaks).  I leak-tested the oiler for 16 hours, with the reservoir brim full with REM oil, laying on it's side, in a polished S.S. pan (no leaks). Then I set the oiler upright in a glass, (to simulate a shirt pocket) for 8 more hours (no leaks).  The only negative I found was the depth of the internal thread. If you could call it a negative, because after all, functionally it worked as intended. So there you go!   Bottom line: This in one nice oiler, much better than I would ever have expected given the price. In fact I plan to buy a second one for backup!   I would not hesitate a moment in recommending the Neiko oiler to anyone!   It's really a no-brainer! The advantages greatly outweigh any disadvantages they're could be. Even if there was a problem, they say you can RMA it an they will have another back to you in no time.    I realize that this is probably not the normal turnaround, but I ordered my Neiko oiler 09/27, the confirmation stated that I would receive it no later than 10/19.  It was in my mailbox on the evening of the 09/30.  From CA to NC! Unbelievable! I bet that won't happen again    All I can say is they must-have-been SMOK'N!

review_headline: didn't do what I expected, left a mess
review_body: I bought this product because of all the glowing reviews; I have a large leather sectional that is about a year old, I wanted to buy a product that would protect this expensive purchase. To be fair, being only a year old there was no signs of wear or aging, I was getting this product to see if I could prevent that. product_title: Koolertron F-12 ELM 327 OBDII PC Car Diagnostic Scanner
review_body:
I purchased this particular ELM327 interface which arrived quickly and the packaging was fine. I plugged it into the car and noticed the diagnostic lights were positioned against the underside of the dash. The device slowly linked up to Torque (Android phone app), and would update very slowly, or freeze up intermittently.

I bought another scanner, only this time it was labeled Soliport ELM 327, and it works flawless.

A few differences I should point out between the two units. I will refer to the problematic scanner as A and the good, working one as B.

- [A] has a nub on the back end of the case, where [B] is flat

- The cut-out notch/tab for the ODBII interface on [B] is on the same side as the label and diagnostic lights

- The product image for [B] showed the cut-out notch/tab being on the same side as the label and diagnostic lights

- [B] syncs up quickly and provides almost instant stats (there is about a fraction of a second delay which was to be expected)

- The mini-CD that comes with [B], arrived in a mini jewel case, while the mini-CD that came with [A] was in a paper sleeve

- When linked via Bluetooth, [A] displayed as CBT, while [B] displayed as OBDII

In conclusion, I am not sure if the first model I purchased was a knockoff or just a different version. Your best bet I think is to search for the \\"Soliport\\" version of this device. Also, ensure that your purchase is fully covered under Amazon's return policy, as you stand a chance of receiving the faulty version.

When removing my cover in late August (less than 3 months old), for a Labor Day camping trip, I noticed the material the cover is made of for the roof area (originally looks very padded with small dots of perforations) was dissolving leaving only the backing material in large areas.      I previously parked my boat in this same shady area and had a boat cover made of \\"Sunbrella\\" material that was custom made in 2002 and even after 9 years, my boat still has this Sunbrella cover in great condition. I have now moved my boat to the other side of the house that is less shady and has more sunlight, and I still bet this Sunbrella material will give me another 9 years of use.    I do not recommend these Expedition covers due to my short, 3 month experience and already seeing the roof material degrading.  I now wonder since Expedition only sells their products through re-sellers on how I will get in contact with Expedition and see how well their \\"3 year warranty, best in the business\\" actually is. product_title: Dorman 674-398 Exhaust Manifold Kit
review_body: I recently purchased a 1998 Ford Expedition 4X4 with the 5.4 Triton engine to replace my older SUV that had seen better days. About a month after getting the Expedition, it developed the notorious exhaust gasket leak these vehicles are well known for. Now the gaskets on this vehicle had been replaced about five years earlier, however, they were now leaking again. Not really wanting to put more money into the truck, but the noise was getting noticeable and somewhat embarrassing.  So after finding a mechanic willing to do the work, I decided to not only replaces the gaskets, but to replace the headers as well. This turned out to be a good decision. (The headers on the truck were rusted quite bad and were near the end of their life anyway) As a side note, I had seriously considered installing shorty style headers with the assumption they might improve my gas mileage. But after talking with numerous people who work on these trucks, they unanimously agreed that shorty headers on this particular vehicle would not be a good investment, and most likely the shorty headers would start leaking again in the near future. So factory style headers it was.  I took these headers to the mechanic and he was very pleased with the appearance of these headers. It took him about 6 hours to replace both passenger and driver side headers along with replacing the studs. I helped speed up this procedure by spraying penetrating oil on all the studs for a week prior to installing the headers. Usually this job can be a royal pain and is not recommended to be taken on by the shade tree mechanic without the proper tools.  The mechanic told me these headers were nearly twice as thick as the factory headers and were very well made. He also said I should not have to worry about these headers for at least ten years. While this is a good truck, and I am sure I will have long sold the truck by then.  The only thing he didn't like were the gaskets that came with the headers. He felt they were a bit cheapand felt they would not hold up long term. He suggested getting the new style Ford gaskets which are made of metal. I told him to install the Ford gaskets as I didn't want to have to have this work done again. Those gaskets are about $120 alone. Not cheap, but considering everything, part of the expense and I shouldn't have to worry about this again.  Since installing the headers, the truck is obviously much, much quieter and I seem to feel a bit of increase in power. Not sure of any mileage gain at this point.  All in all I would highly recommend these headers as a factory style replacement to anyone facing this project with the 5.4 Triton Engine.

product_title: J-B Weld 8277 WaterWeld Epoxy Putty Stick - 2 oz.
review_body:
I've seen several reviews that mention problems with PVC.
PVC is coated with a mold release; fittings are molded,
pipe is extruded, but they all have a mold release compound.
Also, PVC is a hard, non-porous plastic that is very hard
to bind to. Even J-B Weld, which is phenomenal, is a 50/50
proposition IF the PVC isn't cleaned.

Before doing anything with PVC, including gluing, use a PVC
cleaner/primer, always, always, always. Including gluing!
(Hence force, \\"cleaner\\" includes \\"primer\\"), the yellow can.
Don't use purple. It goes on ugly and stays ugly. It's
only used by contractors to prove they primed the pipes.

To paint PVC, wipe it with cleaner to soften it and 10-20
seconds later, wipe it again. Paint it while it's still
tacky. If you're doing a lot, work with only as much as
you can keep tacky. Tacky is the key, work fast.

I tested this with epoxy and it works. I applied
the epoxy while the PVC was tacky with great results. It
may be enough to just clean the PVC and not rush to hit it
while it's tacky but I didn't try that. (J-B Weld works
a day after it's been cleaned).

As for working underwater, hmm, I remain to be convinced.
It did work on a \\"wet\\" gas tank but I first plugged the
leaking holes and then put another layer on the now dry
tank. Then I brushed the entire area with J-B Weld.

I am in no way associated with J-B Weld. I just love it.

product_title: Streetglow SGSW5 5 Position Switch Panel
review_headline: For the price, very very good.
review_body:
First, want to point out that despite the title, this is technically a FOUR position switch panel.
There are 4 separate circuits, as well as a master that turns them all on or off.
The manufacturer calls it a 5 position box, so Amazon wasnt being misleading, they simply continued the error.

Amazon had the cheapest price, cheaper then locally, cheaper then street glow's website.

The product is small, if you cant tell, its about the width of a single DIN stereo, and about half the height.
That may give you a mounting suggestion if you have a vehicle with a 1.5 DIN or 2 DIN stereo thats been replaced with an aftermarket unit.

Its currently mounted under-dash in my dakota. It comes with both screws and a pre-attatched block of 3m high strength tape.
The tape lasted about a week after some really rough handling, and from what i can tell, the entire block of tape wasnt secure on the dash, so thats why it likely failed, plus we had some pretty extreme temperature changes.
I have since reattached it with the tape AND the screws, and it probably wont come off again.

The amazon ad does not specify the amperage rating, its 3 amps per switch for a total of 12, as specified on the package.
If your needs exceed that, a simple relay is easy to wire.
Just to be simple, a pair of 55 watt lights draws up to 9 amps... so you'd want to use a relay if you're going to use this to turn on driving lights.

I've been pretty impressed with this product thus far, especially its small size, and ease of wiring.
The switches are standard size holes, so if one ever fails, replacing it should be easy.
It seems well built, which is unusual for the ricer market, but that makes me happy.
The red indicators are bright enough to be seen during the day, but not obnoxious at night.

Great product. I'm extremely happy with it.

product_title: PIAA  Style Plasma Ion Crystal Yellow 1
review_body: WARNING ~~~ These bulbs are not pure yellow!     In my past three cars (subaru x 2, audi x 1) I have spliced the wiring system so that I can run the fog lights with the parking lights and no main headlamps.    I ski a lot (ski instructor) and I have driven in multiple whiteouts in the dark. The only way to go forward is to turn off all white lights and run with the parking lights + fog lights (if they are yellowed). My last two cars used yellow coated fog light bulbs. The light was very yellow and worked extremely well.    These bulbs are not pure yellow. They transition in this order, white light on the outermost fringe of the beam (about 0% - 10%, which converts to diffraction light blue to pinkish light from about 10% - 20% of the beam, then you get yellow light from 20% until you reach the other side of the beam. So the result is that only about 60% of the light beam is yellow.    If you are after a fancy look, this is probably a pretty cool effect. If you are after the usefulness of yellow light in fog or snow, these are not the best option. A yellow film over the fog light lens is probably a better solution.

product_title: Knox Gilet Air Vest - Medium/Black
review_headline: Probably one of the best pieces of armor to wear
review_body:
Knox Gilet Air Vest, Medium

I've high sided once and had another brand of chest protector (Icon Field Armor). Even though the chest protector was small, the rubber center piece took the impact and I could feel something jabbing at my chest as I flipped over the handlebar. Luckily nothing happened other than hurt my pride and shook my confidence for a few moments. But it was important to have good coverage of the center of the chest. Most racing suits have pads that leave a huge gap in the center (by the zipper) but the Knox chest protector is probably the best chest protector to get according to my local shop. After trying the Knox chest protector + Contour back protector, the numerous straps did not impress me. The Gilet Air vest seems far more streamlined and modern, and even uses the SAME armor as the chest protector (CE Level 1 rated) and the Contour back protector (CE Level 2).

I'm 6 feet, 150 lb, and went with the size MEDIUM Gilet Air vest with the touring back protector. I wear the Knox Cross action shorts with the coccyx armor, so with the Contour, it essentially has the same back coverage as the Contour Race (with the longer tail section). I wear the Gilet Air vest inside my racing suit, so it was important to get the right size suit that would fit this thick vest. My chest without any clothes is about 38\\" in circumference, with the Knox Gilet Air vest, it was about 43\\" in circumference. I tried different sizes of the Gilet Air vest and the Medium fit the best. The small rode up too high on my neck, and the Large had too large of a gap underneath the chest protector.

The Gilet Air vest is not washable, unfortunately. The only thing you could wash is the holder for the chest protector, but I highly recommend wearing a wicking inner suit anyhow. Even if you could only afford something like the Icon Field armor, I still recommend some type of chest and back protector on the inside of an armored jacket or suit.

If you wear the Gilet Air vest in the summer, airflow is essential to cooling your body. I can feel a lot of heat retained behind the chest protector at low speeds, but once air gets to flow through the holes, it is a lot more hospitable.

Overall: 5/5 stars, came highly recommended by a local shop run by riders who practically live at the trackou wear the Gilet Air vest in the summer, airflow is essential to cooling your body. I can feel a lot of heat retained behind the chest protector at low speeds, but once air gets to flow through the holes, it is a lot more hospitable.

Overall: 5/5 stars, came highly recommended by a local shop run by riders who practically live at the track

review_headline: Less Expensive = More Work Required By You
review_body: Less Expensiveterm performance of the clarifier: the clear liquid which is applied as the final step in the restoration process. The clarifier does two things: Its shiny, clear makeup clarifies or virtually erases the dull appearance the plastic lens has very much like the way acrylic floor finish brightens up and shines a dull floor. The other thing the clarifier does is provides UV protection to the lens. I don't have enough data yet to state whether any of the brands uses a superior clarifying solution to any of the others. I can tell you that no matter which one you choose to purchase, you need to go one step further and apply a good, heavy coat of Caranauba wax to your freshly restored lenses. This will help resist the yellowing exponentially as well as to help protect the micro-thin layer of clarifier you applied.     The bottom line is this: You will achieve the same results no matter which of the brands you choose. The amount of work you will be required to do is in direct proportion to the cost of the product.     TIP: No matter which brand you choose to purchase, it's vital that you do not get the freshly restored lens wet for several hours after applying the clarifier. It's best to let it cure overnight and then apply the wax I mentioned above prior to the lenses being exposed to water.

review_headline: I could be mistaken but this product needs improvement.
review_body:
I should have written a review on this product sooner so the first reviewer wouldn't have had to suffer the same fate I did. My apologies to you. This is why it's important for Amazon shoppers to write product reviews to share what they liked or disliked about things they bought. It will save despair for other shoppers and hopefully be saved yourself as well. Now on to the lousy review!

The pad sort of does what it claims to do, just not very well. Maybe my expectations were higher than what was delivered, but I was a bit disappointed nevertheless. I have a obsidian black-colored car that has a nasty knack of showing every little defect in the paint, right down to the tiniest of scratches. I swear, this is the last time I'll purchase a black colored car ever again!

What was wrong with this pad?

First of all, you need to use an obscene amount of clay so that it is thick enough (or is it high enough?) to make good contact with the car's surface. The clay flattens out quickly as you use this with the buffing machine. When the clay gets too flat, you are pretty much buffing with only the applicator pad. Therefore you need to check the thickness level of the clay fairly often.

Second, the inner cavity has a sticky/tacky surface which is supposed to hold the clay. It does an average job at doing that. We as consumers need more stick!!!! In case you are wondering what kind of clay I'm using, I use two types: [[ASIN:B0009IQYEO Meguiar's C-2100 Professional Detailing Clay, Aggressive]] and [[ASIN:B001O7I7JE Meguiar's G1001 Smooth Surface Clay Bar]]. Maybe someone has a better experience using a different brand? If so, please comment or share your own review stating what you are using. We want to know!

product_title: Sunforce 22010 12-Watt Folding Solar Panel
review_headline: No, I didn't own one, but...Now I do
review_body:
This is another example of Amazon's tendency to toss all reviews into the same pot in a \\"close enuff is good enuff\\" kinda way.

Just thought I'd point out that there are two models of this product - 6.5 watt and 12 watt. The 6.5 watt model is named \\"12-VOLT\\". 12 watt is named \\"12-WATT\\" and costs about twice as much (logical, since it is has twice the panel surface). You can tell which one is being reviewed, if you happen to notice \\"Volt\\" or \\"Watt\\", but it is easy to miss unless you previously stumbled onto the \\"option\\" button on the product page.

The \\"12-Volt\\" fella producing 6.5 watts puts out a little under half an amp current. A nice trickle charge for smaller gadgets. The \\"12-Watt\\" model puts out almost one amp. This would charge smaller gadgets faster and provide a reliable charger for, say, a motorcycle battery. Either would get a car battery to a useable level after a while, and keep a charged battery topped off safely, but would not to provide a (car battery) full charge in short time.

Personally, I am glad I stumbled onto the difference, because I think perhaps it would be worth the extra money, and weight, to be able to charge things a little quicker.

I'll have to come back with a \\"real\\" review when I have owned one for a while. For now, I give it 4 stars just because 7 of the previous 8 reviewers gave it at least that. I should remind the reader that this is the small one, although this review ended up with the big one.

---------------- May 16, 2012

Okay, I'm back. I had forgotten my promise until I received the email for the comment asking where my \\"real\\" review is. (Thanks, Y. Li)

Got the smaller one. Not sure why, after reading my comment that I was figuring I'd rather have the larger. I think perhaps the larger wasn't in stock when I was ready to purchase.

Whatever the case, used it on several multi day camping trips to keep a portable 12v \\"Power Tank\\" charged when a.c. wasn't convenient at the campsite. I deliberately discharged the battery (its a big flashlight, too), then charged it up. I also used the \\"iPod/iPhone connector to charge the iPad, although I had to make sure the solar panel stayed in the sun while the iPad stayed in the shade.The iPad never showed it was being charged, but it never does when connected to a USB port, either, and still charges, quite slowly, of course. This is probably about equivalent.

Don't recall specifics, like how long it took to recharge the battery (about a motorcycle battery size), which was mainly used to power my Celestron Telescope until I got the iPad. I believe it took all day in fairly strong sunlight to charge. I had a voltmeter connected to the battery, and it didn't take much of a cloud to cause a drop in voltage. Also, early morning or late evening it was pretty useless, although it could still provide a charge for an almost dead battery, but that is to be expected.

I also had the panel hooked up to the battery as I was running the iPad (via a car 12v adaptor plug). With the voltmeter connected, I could see when the panel was getting snuff light to charge, when it was just able to maintain the charge, and when the iPad was actually drawing down the battery. Basically, it showed full bright sunlight could charge under the iPad's load, but any cloud, or setting sun couldn't keep up.

As far as I'm concerned, the solar panel has proven quite functional for my purposes, and is a keeper. And since it functions as I need it to, I upped it to 5 stars.

product_title: Leather Honey Leather Conditioner, Best Leather Conditioner Since 1968. For Use on Leather Apparel, Furniture, Auto Interiors, Shoes, Bags and Accessories. Non-Toxic and Made in the USA!
review_headline: Used it on five products, and now going to buy more used leather!
review_body:
Leather Honey. I mean, who would have thunk it. This stuff, and there is an official website for Leather Honey, but it doesn't give much more information about it than here in the reviews... for instance, what is it? It's not honey, but it feels like honey. It's not a cleaner, as you have to clean the leather before using it (unscented, disposable baby wipes are touted by professionals, and guess what, they work fantastically!). It is a leather conditioner, ah, I see said the blind man.

I recently bought a few used leather items, a couple of Coach messenger bags, a jacket, etc., from eBay. They were in reasonable shape when I bought them, but just drizzling on some LH, which does feel thick like bee's honey but is perfectly clear, made the leather supple and natural and it felt great. I threw on two or three coats, and although I thought I overdid it with the last one, as the leather was very slippery feeling, like a snake's leathery skin, I just left it overnight and the honey was absorbed (or evaporated, I can't tell) and the bag was supple as a baby's buttocks. Even the LH website says it can;t be overused, but that the excess just needs to be wiped off. I use a dedicated rag for this job, and it is sort of oily on your hands and things, so get ready for that. I did it on my granite kitchen countertop, and it looked like an oily mess when I was done, but cleaned up well.

product_title: Battery Tender Jr. Battery Charger
review_body:
I have a motorcycle and a supercar that I drive infrequently and decided to purchase two Battery Tenders to keep the batteries charged to avoid surprises when I want to drive them only to find the battery dead.

I did a custom install on both vehicles to semi-permently install the battery-charging interface cable so that it is always available and requires only plugging in the Battery Tender. This task was easy and took only a few minutes for the motorcycle and a bit longer for the supercar -- which is not surprising as everything takes longer in a car that is barely 40 inches tall.

The chargers work more or less as advertised, though when I used one to charge my sedan's battery, it never was able to show fully charged with a steady green light. I don't know why that is. The battery is new and the Battery Tender worked correctly the first time, but failed the second time.

The real disappointment is these units are real electricity drains. They run very hot and never shut off regardless of battery charge status, sucking electricity constantly. I was very surprised as these units are described as 'intelligent' designs. It would be simply enough to include a circuit that occasionally checks the battery status and then shuts the unit off. I am not so happy that I have these electricity drains on constantly, so I wind up unplugging and replugging them in often, essentially defeating the purpose. I could do the same with my regular battery charger, which charges must faster and costs nothing.

I can't recommend these chargers because of this power-wasting design. It's very disappointing the design is so poor and could be easily corrected.

product_title: K&N 69-3516TTK Typhoon Performance Intake System
review_body: I've used K&N products before, and some aspects of this intake system meet with my expectations.  It took about an hour to install and did exactly what it advertised - a slight improvement in mileage.  I was surprised that K&N had mis-specified a few of the items that come with the kit.  While not critical, it was odd that the one hose wasn't larger on one end than the other.  There is one hose that is pressed onto one fitting - and it is tight - and then it is to be pressed onto another fitting that is probably 1/4\\" larger in diameter.  It DOES fit and it DOES work, but it's odd that a company as good as K&N would not supply a hose that is larger on one end.  Additionally, I had to source my own hose clamps for a different hose because the two supplied with the kit seemed too small.  I'm sure they would have worked but I didn't feel like wasting the time trying to get them to fit so I used two larger hose clamps that I had in my garage.    As far as how it works, it works fine once installed.  The mileage on the Focus hasn't increased by 10 mpg, but there was an increase of 1 to 2 mpg.  It's noisier than the stock intake (obviously) but it is not noisy at cruising speed on the highway.  Additionally, the noise that it makes isn't unpleasant.  The intake does create a stumble at very low RPM.  When puling from a little under 1,500 RPM to around 1,800 RPM there is a slight stutter.  People with automatic transmissions will never experience this.    Basically, it's well worth the money.  I spent $100 less than my local Advance Auto parts wanted.  There are no drawbacks to this kit, just a few things that raised an eyebrow during the installation.  I'd still just it a five out of five.

(originally written for a solar power forum, but applies here too)

OK, I wussed out, and bought a commercial product! We have a small sleeping hut built on the ranch now, but no power in it yet. It's going to take a while to mount a panel, batteries, charge controller, wire up lights and such, and we arrive at nighttime, and no where to plug the CPAP in ! So I spent a couple days pricing out different ways to accomplish this, and settled on a portable jump start pack. Found a model with good reviews (Peak PKC0AZ 450), and no air compressor (that often fails after 50 total minutes of use). Located one in stock at local autoparts store, and bought it, taking a chance it's been parked in a warehouse for a year, and then in the back room for 2 more years, resulting in a flat, sulfated battery. (fully half of the complaints at Amazon)

Other choice was to get a AGM battery, rig up a case, cigar jack outlet, charger and hope it still fits into the car.

Upon opening it up, and throwing a voltmeter on it, I was pleased to find it reading 12.85V on a warm afternoon. It's built-in indicator showed it was 4/5 charged - also good. I plugged it's wall wart (transformer, not switcher, 12V, .5A) in, and let it top it off for a couple hours, it came to quiescence at 13.37v, and I unplugged it. After an hour, it read 13.13V. Awesome! And the Respironics power cord (for the CPAP) appears to fit snugly into the Lighter jack.

Using my kill-a-watt before I was shopping, I'd discovered that the CPAP consumed about 75 watt hours in a 6 hour run, and that for 2 nights, I'd consume about 12.5 ah of battery. The \\"450A packs\\" claim to have an 18AH AGM battery in them, but I figured, I may as well have a portable unit, than a hulk that will last me a month. And if I only ran it one night (6.25 AH consumed) and then recharged, it'd live a long lifetime. Well, the power brick for the CPAP is a pig. After running all night (6 hours) , the voltage in the AM, read 12.66v Whoo hooo! Internal battery indicator LEDs still showed 4/5 charge, way less drain than the power brick used (all my testing is done with humidifier OFF) so even though the brick read about 3 watts idle, it was using more with a light load.

So, this will recharge at my shop, and I think I'll get a plug in lamp timer, and set that for a 1 hour charge daily, to keep it topped off between visits. And since the shop is on solar power, now my CPAP is too!

Added benefit, the power pack has a LED lamp built in, and a USB power port, so I don't even need a cigar plug Y cord to charge my phone and PDA.

So, I've owned this less than 2 days, but I think it will do the job I need it to, and it's not DOA out of the box. product_title: CURT 13591 Class 3 Trailer Hitch
review_body: A very well built hitch.  The construction quality seems top notch; good looking welds and a nice powder coat.  The price is great too; about $60 cheaper than my local truck shop without labor.  It's not complicated to install so long as you read up a little first.  Also; add a torque wrench to your cart if you haven't bought this yet; you'll need it.    I had a fairly straight forward install on a 2006 Saturn Vue, but my bumper frame seemed to be tweaked or just barely fit; but I managed.  The instructions are overly simplified and for many vehicle makes, so use some imagination.  Like removing the entire bumper fascia and don't skip the very important step of snagging the spacer/bolt plates through your bumper frame even if you see square cutouts for carriage bolts.  The steel is too thin to prevent the head from twisting or pulling through.    A second set of hands and a floor jack is helpful to support the hitch while you're trying to wrangle the side bolts in.  The instructions tell you to clean the threads of the weldnuts on your vehicle frame, but that's an understatement. The amount of crud that can accumulate in there can make it impossible to start a bolt while trying to line up the slots -- completely scrub your threads with a wire brush and lots of WD-40, then thread the included hardware to ensure it pushes all the dirt out.  I had to do this twice on some of mine.  As long as you tighten everything evenly a little at a time; the hitch will pull itself (and your frame?) into position.  Final torque your bolts and it's done.    When installed, this hitch completely blends in with the look of the Saturn and doesn't stick out past the bumper fascia.  I fully recommend it.

product_title: Mobil 1 20W-50 V-Twin Motorcycle Motor Oil
review_headline: The best oil for your V-Twin
review_body:
If you drive an air cooled V-Twin H-D or other make, this this in my opinion the best stuff. When I'm stuck in traffic feeling the heat coming off my air-cooled engine, I feel confident knowing this stuff performs very well at high temperatures. It also helps keep the motor, at least what it seems, a little cooler than the others.

For my bike I would trust SYN3 and Mobil 1, but my first choice is Mobil 1. I don't trust AMSOIL enough to put it in my engine. Here is why. First, AMSOIL 20W50 is not API certified and may void my warranty. The AMSOIL website says its 20W50 meets API requirements, but this doesn't mean it's API certified. If you go to the API website and check AMSOIL, only 8 of their oils are certified, 20W50 is not on the list. Second, I don't trust their multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. Why does this matter? Well, they have literally thousands of distributors. Chances are, if you are reading a blog about how well AMSOIL performs, a \\"news\\" article, product review, comparison, etc., you can most likely trace the source of all these resources (or get directed towards) an AMSOL distributor sponsored website. Even most of the positive AMSOIL posts on discussion boards are pretty much spam promoting the product. Hence, most of the great reviews I've read are not really reviews. I would be very interested to see a quality product review tested by an independent.

As for the H-D SYN3, this is comparable to M1, but because it says H-D on the box, you're gonna pay more for what I believe is at best on par with the Mobil 1. Screamin' Eagle SYN3 is manufactured by Citgo. I heard a rumor on the H-D boards that Harley-Davidson could not strike a deal with Mobil because Mobil would not remove their name from the package.

Mobile 1, just like SYN3, is also approved to lubricate the primary/tranny (in my case, the same compartment), but I've heard mixed thoughts on this. Right now I do have M1 in the primary/tranny with no issues, but am looking at alternatives. However, I'm 100% sold on using M1 as the first choice for my motor.t alternatives. However, I'm 100% sold on using M1 as the first choice for my motor.

product_title: Sunforce 39305 650-Watt High-Efficiency Polycrystalline Solar Power Kit
review_body: [[ASIN:B002BE2FE2 Sunforce 39305 650-Watt High-Efficiency Polycrystalline Solar Power Kit]]    This appears to be a good product, but I have issues with the technical descriptions:  I'd like to see the Product description edited. Although this is billed as a 650 watt kit and is shown with 5 panels, the Product description at the bottom states there are only 3 panels (at 130 Watts each). Additionally, the top-section general description states a 50 amp controller, the bottom section indicates only a 30 amp controller.    For my following comments, I have used basic electricity formula of Power(P) (in Watts) = Current(I) (in Amps) times Voltage(E) (in Volts) or P=IE  The 50 Amp controller is described as being able to handle 750 watts and allows expansion of the system. But since 5 panels at 130 watts already equals 650 watts (54 Amps at 12 Volts), another 130 Watt panel would be 780 Watts (65 Amps at 12 Volts, somewhat above the rated capacity either in Watts or Amps, whichever you choose to use for the description.    My final comment and question is that this system is described as being ideal for 12 Volt charging, but that it automatically switches for 12 or 24 volts. So is the output of the solar panels nominally 24 Volt, with the controller determining final output to the battery? My guess is that it's only a 12 Volt output (650W/12V = 54.17A), so what is the purpose of stating it's auto-switching for 24 Volt?    Clarification on all these issues will help customers make appropriate choices.

review_body: The product's frame BUCKLED when I placed it in the rear window of my car on a sunny day...I recently bought this item, and was trying to use the item to maintain the battery in my vehicle.  So, I plugged the item in my cigarette lighter, and placed the item in my rear window.  When I checked on the solar collector, after a day in the sun, I discovered that the plastic frame had buckled (i.e. severely warped), I assume from the heat of the day.  This occurred after 1 day, and the high for the day was about 85-90oF.    I think my experience with this product is ridiculous.  The item is advertised to maintain your vehicle's battery, and the charger comes with a cigarette lighter.  Furthermore, the item is a solar cell, so the item would be expected to be placed in a sunny location. So, of course, it would be expected that the plastic frame would be able to withstand the heat of the rear window of a vehicle.  But, as I found out the product failed at it's expected function of withstanding the heat of a rear window of a vehicle during a sunny day.    From my memory of watching the Mythbusters, and numerous news articles about the internal temperature of vehicles, the temperature of the interior of a vehicle does not exceed 200oF.  Furthermore, from my memory of numerous plastic cooking utensils, numerous plastics are able to withstand upto 350oF, or more.  Therefore, my conclusion is that the plastic selection for the frame is due to negligent manufacturing.

product_title: Mothers California Gold Clay Bar System
review_body: I was very skeptical in the beginning. Came in and tried it. WORKED flawlessly!  Tree sap on my car had been there ever since I bought my lexus used 3 years ago. I broght it to a local detail shop, and they said it will cost $200 to remove all the tree sap. I declined the service. I tried to just set my mind to ignore all the rough surfaces on my car's body.  When I found this item on Amazon, I watched their ad video, and bought it.  Came in on time, and did exactly what the video said to do.  First, shampooed my car thoroughly. Waited until dry completely.  Sprayed that detail soln came with the whole box.  Started rubbing gently, and I could feel that resistance while it was gliding.  Kept gliding circularly, and finally started feeling smoothness.  Dried with enclosed towel. It was amazing. I never knew my lexus paint was that shinny. I could even see good detail of my face.  Took about good 30min to shave all that gunky sticky(mine was almost permanently hardened)tree sap, Dried good and applied those quick liquid wax then buffed.  I saved literally more than $200 for what they call a professional job. Well, it's not anymore.  It's a DIY job. This is by far the greatest invention I had experienced recently. Thank you Mothers.  Now there are many other manufacturers who have similar approach. Well, this Mothers just has all that you needed to do the sap removal.  FYI, you probably well use all the clay that comes with this box. If you have more than one car, I would probably get more sets of clay. Oh, remember, if you happened to drop the clay on the floor while you are working, just throw it away.  Plus, Mothers recommend to do this job at a shaded area. I guess sun might cause slight damage to the paint while you work on it. I washed my car during the day, and clayed at night in my garage.  You will love this product.

product_title: Accutire MS-4710B Motorcycle 5-99 PSI Digital Tire Gauge
review_body:
I needed a replacement for my 10 year old digital tire gauge, so I thought I'd find something that would really meet my needs. Since I ride a motorcycle most of the time, and on long distant rides, tire pressure is something that if not done right will ruin your trip.

I was going to get a backlit version, but saw this one. Accessing my R1200RT rear tire's valve is a bit difficult with the panniers and double brake discs. This looked like a good buy.

Highlights

1. Seems accurate. I tried several analog and digital gauges on my car, and this was spot on. I tried it on my bike, and apparently, I need some air!
2. Battery appears to be replaceable, which was the issue with my trusty old one.
3. Handle grip is nice.
4. Huge numerals for those who have poor near vision.

The not so highlights

1. It's plastic. Sure, that makes it light and probably cheap to make, but I suspect that 90º bend is going to be a problem. You might torque it a bit getting it off the valve stem, which might break it. But it hasn't broken yet, but I'm concerned.
2. It's hard to read in the dark. Make that next to impossible. OK, I could have purchased another version, but I'm just mentioning it.
3. There is no audible beep when it captures the pressure. But, it's something I'll just have to accept.

Overall, for the price, it appears to be a very well designed gauge for a motorcyclist. Interestingly, I tried it on my car, and the angle precluded me from using it with the numbers facing me.

This gauge isn't perfect, but it's pretty nice. I wish it were all metal, but we'll see if I mess it up. It's now in my tank bag, always available for use.

product_title: ZANheadgear Neoprene Face Mask
review_body:
I got this for my sister and it fit her perfectly. And yes, she looked awesome in it. Then we had a wicked blizzard, with 50 mph winds, and I lost my scarf. So I borrowed it for the shoveling.

It fits my ginormous head just as well as it fit hers. It was surprisingly comfortable to wear for my 3 hour shovel-a-thon. I was able to slip my glasses in through the eye holes so I could see, I got enough air through the nose hole so I didn't pass out, and it somehow even managed to warm the air up a bit. Meanwhile, the snow that was being blown at my face like a sandblaster that literally had me cracked and bleeding within 5 minutes had no effect through this mask.

So to sum up, it really IS one-size-fits-all, it's comfortable, it protects your face and nose and lungs wonderfully, you can wear glasses with it, and it looks incredibly badass. Oh, and it washes easily and the print hasn't been effect yet. And it was priced very reasonably. Five star product all the way.

product_title: Show Chrome Digital 5 Funtion Volt Meter
review_headline: Not suitable for motorcycle use due to lack of water proofing
review_body: I did install this on my bike, however, I'm going to be using RTV and plastic to make the housing waterproof. It's behind the fairing, so hopefully that'll protect it from the worst of the rain.     The biggest gripe I have about this unit, however, is that the backlight is weak to the point of being useless. It consists of a string of SMD green LEDs along one long edge that shoot into a white plastic diffuser behind the LCD. You can see from the product photo how irregular the lighting is, but more importantly it's very, very dim.    As ambient light lessens your eye acclimates, but at some point you can no longer see the display numbers. It isn't until it's completely pitch black before your eye adjusts enough for the backlight to start becoming visible. It's not nearly as bright as your dash lights, or your radio display. The irony is that the packaging offers \\"Strong backlight\\" as one of the selling features. Perhaps they were hoping for placebo effect?    All in all, this is basically a very inexpensive piece of import electronics that, IMHO, isn't worth more than $10 and most definitely isn't suitable for use on a motorcycle without significant modifications.

review_headline: Run, run like the wind in another direction
review_body: I bought this unit because it had everything I wanted. Mainly an internal iPod dock and remote control. If it had worked properly, I would have been 100% happy. It did not. Unfortunately, the unit locks up after being in use for a while (> approx 20 minutes). I have no idea whether this unit was defective or if this was a design flaw inherent in all of them because I got absolutely no response from their Customer Service department to my e-mails, voice-mails or calls.    On 12/01 Roadmaster VR-3's call center message said \\"... large call volume... over 25 minute hold times...\\", but I was on hold for 3.5 hours... REALLY?!?!?!?... nobody there found the time to answer the phone in 3.5 hours. That is 100% unacceptable.     Also, I called on a Monday at 9:30 est and their call center message said they were closed then disconnected me, despite being within the office hours defined in the same message.     I left 3 text messages on their website's customer service section, and only got an automated response - after 3 weeks nobody had contacted me as promised.    Lastly I opted out of the call center and left a voice mail with an explanation and my number - no call back.    Bottom line - Their customer service is horrendous. I really rate them 0 stars.    Ironically, I really liked the product and would have kept it if I could have solved the problem or determined if a replacement would have worked.

product_title: Lincoln Lubrication Grease Gun Holder Grease Needle Nozzle and Coupler
review_body: First grease gun I've ever bought and I wanted it also to be the last.    Having read all the reviews here before I ordered, I was aware of the \\"issues\\" with the tight zerk coupler and difficult priming. I experienced neither with my gun. I took the coupler off the hose and loosened it before I installed the hose on the gun. Also, after loading the grease cartridge, I primed the gun before putting on the hose giving several pumps until I started to see liquid appear at the hose fitting. After attaching the hose, I continued priming but it seemed that I wasn't getting anywhere. So, I loosened the bulk fitting on the head slightly and some air was released as it opened. I tightened it back hand tight and continued priming until I could tell the grease was at the coupler. Didn't take long at all and went to work greasing my lawn tractor.    Worked like a champ! A couple of zerks were slightly tight but as someone else mentioned, a firm tug on the coupler and it came right off. No need to tighten the coupler while on the zerk either. I simply held the coupler firmly on the zerk and pumped away. I could feel the pressure this gun was putting out. One hand operation of the gun is a snap. Only trouble I had was getting the coupler on one of the zerks in the steering linkage - no fault of Lincoln as this is a John Deere design flaw so now I'm on the hunt for a different coupler that will sneak into that tight spot. Do highly recommend using the hose instead of the pipe. I didn't even have to try the pipe to figure out it would be much more difficult to use for this application.    Only thing I would do differently if I had to start all over is put some teflon tape around the thread joints since a small amount of grease leaked out between the hose and coupler. Maybe that would've stopped it...?    Go ahead and buy it - its worth the little bit of extra money...

product_title: 3M 39008 Headlight Lens Restoration System
review_body: Okay, so this is an \\"almost 5 star\\" product, but I have some tips about things that could have been included in kit or mentioned in instructions that would have made this a 5 star kit.    ***REVIEW***  3M makes some of the best sand paper and this kit comes with very high quality 3M 500 grit, 800 grit discs and a special 3000 grit finishing sand pad. Everything attaches via hook & loop (velcro) to the pad that attaches on end of a drill. You start with the \\"rougher\\" 500 paper, progress to the 800 paper to make the scratches on the lens finer, and then end the sanding part with the 3000 grit pad that is so fine that it buffs the 800 grit scratches. The last step is a 3M foam pad with 3M headlight paste that polishes the lens. The end result is definitely an impressive improvement.    ***TIPS THAT WERE EITHER NOT MENTIONED OR EMPHASIZED IN KIT***  o   First, the drill... yes, a cheap cordless drill may not have the RPM and longevity to do 2 headlights, but higher-end cordless drills will likely have both the RMP and longevity to do a pair of headlights. I started with a good Li-Ion cordless and ended with a corded Dewalt... but note, with the extra RPM of a corded drill, an inexperienced DIY'er could \\"over do it.\\"  o   Second, and these are tips not necessarily mentioned in the kit, you need to protect your paint from the sanding discs. The discs are round, and much of the area around your lenses is straight. If you're not careful, you can end up with some big paint scuffs. So, tape up the area around the lens well, open your hood up so you have extra room to maneuver and don't bump the chuck of your drill on the painted hood, and here is my special **tip** I tore off one of the flaps of some cardboard boxes and jammed them over the tape and under the light. This works great because if you are using, especially, a corded drill, the RPM on drill is enough to tear through even a double layer of tape.    ***FINAL ANALYSIS***  Considering the ridiculous price of a new headlight lens vs. the $15 - $20 cost of a reconditioning kit like the 3M, and given the low level of difficulty in the refinishing job... I highly recommend this kit (even if I didn't give it 5 stars).

product_title: Hawk Performance HB530F.570 HPS Performance Ceramic Brake Pad
review_body:
Replaced my OEM pads with these. Definite improvement in stopping distance and absolutely no squeal or noise from these. I spent a lot of time researching what to replace my OEM pads and these where the ones I settled on. While there were options at a third the cost of these performance was my only consideration. They come with a packet of high temperature grease to use between the pads and backing plate and on any pins that may need lubricant.

A few notes to remember when replacing. Get your rotors turned down or replaced if needed. If they are in decent shape (not grooved or glazed) you can sand the surface with 120 grit sandpaper. You need to do at least one of these things as the pads will not bed-in properly with the rotors.

After installation the following is the proper bed-in procedure recomended by hawk to bring the resins out of the pad and mix in with the rotor surface. Here is the proper way to bed-in these pads after installation. This is very important to do after you first install the new pads:

After installing new brake pads, make 6 to 10 stops from approximately 30-35 mph applying moderate pressure.
Make an additional 2 to 3 hard stops from approximately 40 to 45 mph.
DO NOT DRAG BRAKES!
Allow 15 minutes for brake system to cool down.
After step 4 your new pads are ready for use.

Update 11/4/2010: Have several thousand miles on the pads now. Absolutely no noise and they still grab great. No regrets on choosing these. Also noticed that these have less dust buildup on the wheels versus the OEM pads that came on the car.

Update 7/2/2013. I now have about 23k miles one these pads. Just checked them tonight and there is still 65-70% of the lining left (the original OEM pads on my type S lasted 22k miles which from forums I read is typical). Stopping power still great. I replaced my OEM rear pads with Hawks HPS ones as well recently (though they were not that worn). The minimal break dust has kept the rims very nice. Well worth the extra cost for these pads based on better performance, longer lasting and significantly less brake dust on the rims (easily less than half the dust of what the oem pads left on the rims).

product_title: EZ-Pass Clip Electronic Toll Tag Holder for E-ZPass / i-Zoom / i-Pass - BLACK
review_body: I've been using one of these (same brand/model) for several years now, though I bought mine at an auto parts store.  This is more of a \\"long term\\" review.  I have the black one.    I live in PA, and use it with the EZ Pass tag we have here.  I have no issues with the fitment of the tag in the holder; it fits great, and does not rattle at all.  The holder then uses 3 small suction cups to adhere to the windshield, and I place mine behind the rear view mirror so that it's out of sight and does not create a blind spot.  I have no problems with it failing to work properly when secured that way.  That's not to say there aren't any problems, however...    My car is kept outside year round, and is a daily commuter.  Being in NE PA, it sees all weather, from sub zero temps in the winter to over 100 degrees ambient in the summer, and everything in between.  As a result, the included suction cups have yellowed and become less effective over the years, being exposed to so many temperature variants.  That, in and of itself, isn't really a big deal, but it does mean that the tag regularly falls off of the windshield, hits the dash, and bounces somewhere in the car.  Sometimes this happens while driving, causing me to have to fish around for the tag so that I can get through the tolls, and sometimes it happens while parked.  Sometimes it's a result of the heat, and sometimes of the cold.  Sometimes, the cups won't stick due to condensation on the inside of the windshield.  Fortunately, it hasn't damaged my dash at all, but for those who have expensive nav screens and whatnot in their dash, falling objects could be a problem.  So, that's problem number one.    Problem number two is even more prevalent, and contributes to the falling problem, and that's heat.  In the sun/heat, the plastic melts.  It doesn't melt where the tag slips in; rather, it melts where the suction cups attach to the tag, turning those points into a hot, gooey mess.  This results in two things: first, the holes that the suction cups go in become enlarged over time as the plastic continues to melt, day in and day out, which contributes to the holder falling off of the windshield more often since it's not as secure.  Second, because the plastic becomes a hot, gooey mess, the holder will fall off, land on a seat, and the melted plastic will stick to the seat, making a mess that needs cleaning, while the suction cups will remain stuck on the windshield.  This requires you to reattach the cups to the holder, further deforming the melted holes since the plastic is usually still soft.    The third problem is a minor one that most people won't encounter, and that's that the design of the holder (using 3 suction cups) doesn't allow it to be used on curved surfaces.  This means that I can't stick it on the inside of my curved motorcycle windshield on my sport bike.  If it were the 2 bigger suction cup design, I could rotate it and mount it vertically, but the 3 small suction cups prevents it from working like that.  Again, not a problem for most people, but fellow riders know that digging for an EZ Pass tag while riding through the tolls is a huge pain, and potentially very dangerous, so it would be nice if one didn't have to think about doing that.  Even if I could stick it on the bike windshield, the thing is so deformed from the heat now that I'd be afraid it would fall off while I'm riding, and that would really make for a problem.    So, in conclusion, it works, which is why I give it 3 stars, but it fails to withstand the test of time and is very susceptible to temperature/weather conditions, which is why I can't rate it any higher than that.  I have since read of acrylic holders that supposedly do not melt; given the choice, I'd definitely go for one of those now, as this model certainly has a limited lifespan.

product_title: Ogio No Drag Backpack
review_body: All of the reviews here have focused on the utility, construction, ease of use, etc.  All valid points, but I have another kind of feedback to offer.  I was riding my motorcycle on a long trip recently, on a VERY hot day.  I had most of my gear in saddlebags, but I was going to need to work remotely using my company laptop on this trip, so i took along my company laptop, power cords, and a few folders of paperwork in the Ogio No Drag.  When I left home, I had the backpack on as, well, a backpack!  Strapped on my back, as you would usually wear a backpack.  However, my armored riding suit has the back air vent in a place that it is somewhat blocked by any kind of backpack.  Not a flaw of the backpack, really a flaw of the suit itself.  So, I took the backpack off and strapped it to the top of my saddlebags, on top of the seat behind me.  Bungee corded it on, and was on my way. Well, long story short, the bungee cord failed.  The backpack came off somewhere along the Interstate, at speeds between 65-70.  Had no idea when it came off, so assumed I would never see it again.  A few days later, some amazingly honest people called me up and said \\"we found a bag next to an exit ramp with your business card in it\\"!!  When I retrieved the bag, it was scuffed pretty dramatically on the hardshell side.  It had obviously taken quite a tumble and skid across the asphalt,  Good news: all contents, including the laptop, survived without a single scratch!  Almost unbelievable how well the bag held up.  It is still perfectly usable, just with some obvious battle scars!!  I am now much more careful when attaching bags to my bike, but I also am now a true believer in the durability of the Ogio No Drag!!!

product_title: aFe Power Magnum FORCE 54-81172 Toyota Tundra Performance Intake System (Oiled, 5-Layer Filter)
review_body: I have no performance or MPG data as of yet. I installed on a 2010 tundra 5.7L    In terms of sound, little change when cruising or idling but step on the gas and there is a pretty loud growl in the cab. There are various sound files and videos floating around but I don't think they really tell you what it sounds like.    Install: Instructions are nearly useless. Their only utility is that they give you a basic progression of steps. A couple key points when installing (based on my newbie experience):  (1) Just unscrew the mass air flow sensor and leave it attached to the cable rather than trying to unplug the cable then unscrew the sensor from the stock air pipe.  (2) pull the screw and metal pipe out of the rubber grommet that holds the stock filter box in the engine. It makes it easier to get the same rubber grommet back through the holes in the Afe box. Then you can shove the metal tube containing the screw through the rubber grommet.  (3) The 14 inch rubber sealing strip goes around the metal hole between the fender well and the engine compartment. Do not try to put it around the edge of the Afe box that goes into that hole.   (4) Once you have the rubber seal strip in place, the Afe box really just sets up against the hole, it does not tuck into it. At the point at which you have the rubber strip in the hole and the Afe box bolted down (which is not easy to get in place), the Afe box does not sit very stable, it rocks around. But once you have the airflow tube in place, things hold in place.  (5) the most annoying part is trying to shove the part of the Afe box into the fender inlet hole with the rubber seal strip in place. I could not get it to do anything other than sit up against it. This is an annoying design flaw when you consider how easily and well designed the stock filter box is in this regard.   (6) The second most annoying part is trying to screw in the bolts/grommets in the weird locations they are placed in on the Afe box. One is in a deep hole (inside the box) and the other is in a corner. And getting either bolt to settle into the hole requires some pushing and shoving.    In the end, even a total newbie with little or not mechanical ability was able to get it installed in an hour or so and that was after trying 2-3 different ways to try and get the rubber seal to fit.    Have fun. At the end of the day, its a nice product.

product_title: Anchor 3003 Engine Mount
review_headline: 2000 Ford Focus SE DOHC Motor Mount
review_body:
I bought this product last year and installed it myself in my Ford Focus 2000 SE. The noise in the cabin changed dramatically - very quiet. It felt like I was in a new car. However, about 3 months later, the cabin noise increased a bit. I thought the problem was with the motor mount but it turned out to be that the driver side motor mount needs to be changed too. You can tell by the shaking of the driver side mirror. I had the belt changed which required the removal of the motor mount. After the re-installation of the motor mount, the cabin noise became very quiet again, the same as when the motor mount was first installed. I ordered the driver side motor mount and will install it later.

For the price, this product is worth it.

The problem I encountered with the order was that Amazon Part Finder does not have the 2000 Ford Focus SE DOHC (Dual Over Head Cam) listed. So I ordered the mount for the SOHC (Single Over Head Cam) instead and it did not fit. I ordered the 2001 Ford Focus SE DOHC version and it fit. Before ordering any parts on Amazon.com make sure you know what type of vehicle overhead cam you have... DOHC or SOHC. You can also take look at the motor mount in your car and make sure it matches the picture on Amazon.

*************************

This is a followup review... DATE = 9/19/2011

The motor mount broke at the top within a few months of purchase. I had to use a special glue with rubber inserts to hold it in place - so far it has held up. In addition, it has caused the driver-side rear(Anchor) mount to break several times because the broken mount cause a misalignment with the chassis. I agree with the 1 (zero) star review that it is best to buy the OEM product.
